spans.s:
Bhaga denotes a part of the chariot in one passage of the Rigveda according to Hillebrandt.
Foot notes ii. 34, 8.
Vedische Mythologie, 3, 95.
Bhaginī, ‘sister,’ literally the ‘fortunate one’ in so far as she has a brother, occurs in the nirukta (iii. 6).

Bhagī-ratha Aikṣvāka (‘descendant of ikṣvāku’) is the name of a king in the Jaiminīya upaniṣad brāhmaṇa (iv. 6, 1. 2). It is important to note that he is regarded as being on friendly terms with the kuru-Pañcālas, which points to the Ikṣvākus being allied to that people, and not belonging (as is the case in the Buddhist books) to the east of India.

Bhāga-dugha, ‘dealer out of portions,’ ‘distributor,’ is the name of one of the king's ‘jewels’ (ratnin) in the yajurveda Saṃhitās and Brāhmaṇas. What his functions exactly were is uncertain. Sāyaṇa in some places renders the word by ‘tax-collector’ but in others as ‘carver,’ thus making this functionary either a revenue officer or a mere court official.
Foot notes taittirīya Saṃhitā, i. 8, 9 2; kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xv. 4; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, ii. 6, 5; iv. 3, 8; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxx. 13.
taittirīya brāhmaṇa, i. 7, 3, 5; iii. 4, 8, 1; Satapatha brāhmaṇa, i. 1, 2, 17; v. 3, 1, 9.
On taittirīya Saṃhitā and taittirīya brāhmaṇa, loc. cit., and on Śatapatha brāhmaṇa, v. 3, 1, 9.

Bhāga-vitti (‘descendant of Bhagavitta’) is the patronymic of a teacher called Cūḍa or Cūla in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka upaniṣad.
Foot notes Bṛhadāraṇyaka upaniṣad, vi. 3, 17, 18 Mādhyaṃdina.
